doc.title: Joel Dorn interviewed by Monk Rowe, New York City, New York, January 13, 2007

title: Nesuhi Ertegun hands Dorn the jazz producer job
summary: Dorn picked artists to bring to Atlantic. He recalls Nesuhi's roster, his apprenticeship, the independent Rufus Harley record that got him hired, and his first stable of artists.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: Well I just was wondering about the impression some of those bands made on you in those jazz clubs.
Oh, so I go to the clubs and I was starting to pick out the people, if I got to Atlantic Records, well these are the people I was going to take with me, take away from other labels. You know.

Well I mean what is this — a business of — I mean Mother Theresa is not a record producer and doesn’t work at a record company you know, and neither did Bertrand Russell you know. We’re talking about you know like a few labels, a lot of acts, and you know, you’re like putting your money on different horses. So I had my group of guys that I wanted to do. Nesuhi, when he asked me to come to Atlantic full time to become the jazz producer it was because he had kind of run the string on his era. He had John Coltrane and the Modern Jazz Quartet and Ornette Coleman and Herbie Mann and Fathead and Hank Crawford and Ray Charles and Chris Connor and Charles Mingus. That was his time. As Atlantic grew and he became more involved in setting up the European and worldwide operation he wasn’t in the clubs as much. He turned it over to me. I mean I had to produce a lot of records on my own and really jump through a bunch of hoops until, you know, he felt I was ready to start to learn. I mean you have no idea, and I had no idea at the time, what it was to apprentice to a Nesuhi Ertegun. Because I was really a producer with training wheels, you know. And he distributed some of the independent records I had made with Duke Pearson and Sonny Stitt and people like that, and like a jazz bagpipe player from Philly named Rufus Harley.
Yeah, yeah. That got me the job at Atlantic.

That was the first record I made that sold you know. And I would come to his sessions you know, so I’d see him do the MJQ or Herbie Mann or Hank Crawford or Betty Carter. And I was kind of learning as I went along. I didn’t know what I was doing. And when I saw that he was less and less involved in producing jazz, and then when he called me to come to New York and I had no idea what he wanted, and he said, “you know that job you want? Well you’ve got it.” And he said, “I love you, you’re a nice kid” all of that. He said, “you’ll live or die by what you do.” He said, “we’ll always be friends,” he said, “but now is your chance.” So I had my stash of guys. I had Rahsaan, I had Yusef, I brought Fathead back to the label. I had some new ideas for Hank Crawford. I worked with Mose

Allison, you know I worked with Herbie Mann a little bit and then Les McCann and then Eddie Harris. So when he hired me he said, “I’m not in the clubs anymore, this isn’t my time, this is your time, so go get ‘em.”
